podcast.body: Released on January 20, 1991, "Wind of Change" became a worldwide hit, selling an estimated 14 million copies and earning the title of the best-selling single by any German artist. It was particularly successful in the USSR, where it resonated with several generations of fans in Eastern Europe and was believed by some to embody themes of freedom that led to the dissolution of the Soviet Union and authoritarian regimes behind the Iron Curtain. "And when the song was released on January 20, 1991, it became a worldwide hit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: Released on January 20, 1991, this power ballad became a global hit, selling an estimated 14 million copies worldwide, making it the best-selling single by any German artist. The band, originally from Hanover, West Germany, recorded an English version and a Russian version under the name The Vetter Paramen. The song was a massive hit in the USSR, leading to the band presenting Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev with a gold record. It remains highly popular among fans in Eastern Europe, and rumors persist that it was part of a CIA operation to destabilize Soviet society with its message of freedom and revolution. "Wind of Change was a global hit for the Scorpions, a metal bandit of Hanover in what was then West Germany."
